title: Strong-coupling quantum optics in free space with holes in a Fermi sea
authors: Hao Wang, Hayden C. Orth, Duo Xu, Emily J. Davis
abstract: Coherent and efficient light-matter interfaces between an atom and a single mode of the electromagnetic field are essential for quantum technologies. Traditionally, these systems employ optical cavities or waveguides to isolate a specific mode of light, but a more recent approach is to engineer antennas from ordered configurations of trapped ultracold atoms that exhibit controllable and directed scattering. In this work, we propose a method to engineer an antenna from the center-of-mass wavefunction of a single atom, which can produce directed emission and thereby exhibit strong coupling to a target mode of light in free space. We predict that the resulting single-atom cooperativity can be comparable to the current state of the art in optical cavity and waveguide QED experiments. Building on this approach, we show that a wavepacket antenna becomes a single-atom mirror in the linear response regime. We study the modified dipole-dipole interactions and band structure of chains of such emitters, which can exhibit sub- and superradiance at spacings much larger than the wavelength of the light. Extending our approach to multi-level atoms, we propose a method to achieve arbitrary spatial scattering from a single atom, including uni-directional spontaneous emission. Finally, we elucidate how our approach can enhance cooperative scattering in conventional arrays of tightly trapped atoms.
summary: This paper presents a novel method to achieve strong, directed light-matter coupling in free space by engineering an atomic antenna from the wavefunction of multiple trapped fermions. By utilizing Pauli blocking, the authors suppress unwanted inelastic decay channels, enabling deterministic, highly directional spontaneous emission from a single atom. This work offers a pathway to realizing high-cooperativity quantum optics without relying on traditional optical cavities.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving coherent and controlled light-matter interactions in free space, circumventing the need for engineered boundaries like optical cavities.
main_result: The authors propose using quantum statistics (Pauli blocking) on an array of fermions to engineer a single-atom antenna that achieves directed spontaneous emission and high cooperativity in free space.
method: The analysis uses the Green's function approach and master equations, incorporating Pauli blocking effects derived from filling the lowest vibrational modes of a trap.
model_or_system: The system involves an atom trapped in a potential, where the collective behavior of multiple fermions (a Fermi sea) is used to modify the decay channels. The interaction is modeled via the dipole coupling to the free electromagnetic field.
key_observables: Cooperativity (C), directed spontaneous emission rate, and modified dipole-dipole interactions.
important_parameters: Fermion number (N), Lamb-Dicke parameter ($\eta$), and the ratio of elastic to inelastic decay rates.
main_assumptions: The approach relies on the ability of Pauli blocking to suppress inelastic decay channels, forcing emission into the desired elastic channel.
figures_summary: Figures compare point dipole scattering (isotropic) versus antenna/wavepacket scattering (directed), and illustrate the mechanism of suppressing inelastic scattering via Pauli blocking.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from the general need for free-space light-matter coupling, introduces the single-atom antenna concept, develops the theory using fermionic loading and Pauli blocking, and concludes by discussing extensions like arbitrary spatial emission.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses fundamental open quantum system problems by using many-body quantum statistics (Pauli blocking) to engineer quantum optical phenomena (directional emission) in a highly controllable, solid-state-like environment (the trap).
